artworks.title: Acheulean hand axe, Saint-Acheul

location.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.institution: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (North Carolina Archaeological Collection)

artworks.medium: Bifacially knapped flint
artworks.description: The hand axe is the signature tool of the Acheulean, a tradition that early humans sustained for well over a million years across Africa, Europe and Asia. Each one was shaped by striking flakes from both faces of a flint nodule until a symmetrical, teardrop cutting edge remained. This example comes from the gravel pits of Saint-Acheul at Amiens, the site that gave the industry its name, and still bears its 1920s collector's label.
facts: The Acheulean is named after Saint-Acheul, a suburb of Amiens, where hand axes were found in the Somme river gravels in the 19th century.
Hand axes were made from roughly 1.6 million to about 100,000 years ago, chiefly by Homo erectus and its successors, and only rarely by Homo sapiens.
Jacques Boucher de Perthes's finds in the Somme gravels in the 1840s helped establish that humans had coexisted with extinct Ice Age animals.

artworks.title: Löwenmensch (Lion-man) of Hohlenstein-Stadel
artworks.medium: Carved mammoth ivory
artworks.description: A standing figure with a human body and the head of a cave lion, carved from a mammoth tusk with flint tools. Found in fragments in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in the Swabian Jura in 1939, it was reassembled over decades from more than two hundred pieces and is among the oldest known figurative sculptures.
facts: Discovered on 25 August 1939 by Otto Völzing, a week before the Second World War halted the dig.
Radiocarbon dating of its find layer places it between 35,000 and 41,000 years old.
Seven parallel transverse gouges are carved into the left arm; the 2012-13 restoration raised its height from 29.6 to 31.1 cm.

artworks.title: Hand stencils, Leang Pettakere
artworks.medium: red ochre sprayed over the hand
artworks.description: Hands held against the limestone and sprayed with red ochre, in one of the Maros-Pangkep karst caves of southern Sulawesi. A stencil in the neighbouring cave of Leang Timpuseng is at least 39,900 years old, which made the Sulawesi caves the oldest dated figurative rock art in the world when it was published in 2014, older than anything then dated in Europe.
facts: The age comes from uranium-series dating of the calcite 'cave popcorn' that grew over the paintings, which gives a minimum age.
A nearby painting of a Sulawesi warty pig at Leang Tedongnge was later dated to at least 45,500 years.
The stencils are negative images: the hand is the unpainted part.

artworks.title: Panel of the Lions, Chauvet Cave

location.name: Vallon-Pont-d'Arc
location.institution: Grotte Chauvet (sealed; shown from the Grotte Chauvet 2 facsimile)

artworks.medium: charcoal and scraping on limestone
artworks.description: The right part of the Panel of the Lions in the deepest chamber of Chauvet Cave: a pride of lions, drawn without manes, stalks a herd of bison. The charcoal was drawn on a wall first scraped clean, and the artists shaded with their fingers to round the bodies. This photograph is of the full-scale facsimile at Grotte Chauvet 2, since the cave itself has been closed to the public since its discovery in 1994.
facts: Chauvet's oldest drawings are around 36,000 years old, twice the age of Lascaux.
A rockfall sealed the cave about 21,000 years ago, which is why the drawings survive so well.
Werner Herzog filmed the panels in 3D for Cave of Forgotten Dreams (2010).

artworks.title: Venus of Willendorf

madeIn.name: Willendorf II site, Willendorf in der Wachau

artworks.medium: Carved oolitic limestone with traces of red ochre
artworks.description: A palm-sized female figure with exaggerated breasts, belly and hips, a patterned head without a face, and no feet. It was carved from an oolitic limestone not found locally and once tinted with red ochre. Found in 1908 in loess deposits beside the Danube at Willendorf, it is the best-known of the Palaeolithic Venus figurines.
facts: Recovered on 7 August 1908 during a dig led by Josef Szombathy, Hugo Obermaier and Josef Bayer.
Radiocarbon dates from the surrounding layers suggest it was buried about 30,000 years ago.
Its limestone is not local to the Wachau; the name Venus is a modern label, and some scholars prefer Woman of Willendorf.

artworks.title: Megaloceros, Lascaux

location.name: Montignac-Lascaux
location.institution: Grotte de Lascaux (sealed; replica photographed at the Anthropos museum, Brno)

artworks.medium: mineral pigment on limestone
artworks.description: A giant deer with its enormous antlers thrown back, painted in black manganese with a red ochre ground and a line of black dots beneath. It stands near the end of the Axial Gallery of Lascaux, among the horses and aurochs that made the cave famous after four teenagers found it in 1940. The cave was closed in 1963 because visitors' breath was growing algae and calcite over the paintings; this is a museum replica.
facts: Megaloceros giganteus, the Irish elk, carried antlers up to 3.6 metres across and died out about 7,700 years ago.
Lascaux holds about 600 painted animals and nearly 1,500 engravings.
The dots and squares scattered around the animals have never been decoded.

contributed.note: Import from Wikimedia Commons; photograph of a museum replica, released to the public domain by the photographer

artworks.title: Lascaux, the great deer (facsimile panel)

date.label: c. 17,000 years ago (the painting); facsimile 20th century

artworks.medium: Cast of the cave wall with the painting reproduced; original in manganese and ochre on limestone
artworks.description: A piece of the cave wall you can stand in front of: a scan of a facsimile panel of one of Lascaux's great deer, a stag with its antlers thrown back, painted about 17,000 years ago in a few sure strokes of black manganese, with the rock's own bulges used for the body. Lascaux has been closed to visitors since 1963, when the breath of a thousand people a day began to grow algae and mould on the paintings, so the cave is known today through casts and facsimiles like this one, in the Anthropos Pavilion in Brno. The photograph beside it shows the Megaloceros in the cave itself.
facts: Lascaux holds some 600 painted animals and nearly 1,500 engravings, found in 1940 by four teenagers and a dog named Robot.
The painters worked by lamplight, on scaffolding in the higher galleries, with pigments ground from manganese oxides and iron ochres.
The casts are made from precise surveys of the wall so that the relief the painters used, a bulge for a shoulder, a crack for a line, is kept.

artworks.title: Polychrome ceiling, Altamira

location.name: Santillana del Mar
location.institution: Cueva de Altamira (closed; reproduction photographed at the Deutsches Museum, Munich)

artworks.medium: ochre and charcoal on limestone
artworks.description: The great ceiling of Altamira, where a herd of bison is painted in red ochre and outlined in black over the natural bulges of the rock, so that each animal stands out as if in relief. Found in 1879 by Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola and his young daughter María, it was the first Palaeolithic cave art recognised as such, after two decades of scholars dismissing it as a forgery. The cave is closed to protect the paintings; this is the full-size reproduction in Munich.
facts: The polychrome bison date to around 14,500 years ago; the oldest marks in the cave are over 35,000 years old.
The ceiling is about 18 metres long and was painted lying down, under a roof little more than a metre high.
Picasso is often quoted as saying that after Altamira, all is decadence.

artworks.title: Polychrome ceiling of Altamira (replica)

location.name: Munich
location.institution: Deutsches Museum (replica; the original is in the Cave of Altamira)

artworks.medium: Replica of a painted limestone cave ceiling: ochre and charcoal on rock, reproduced in relief
artworks.description: The great ceiling of Altamira, where a herd of bison is painted in red ochre and outlined in black over the natural bulges of the rock, so that each animal stands out as if in relief. Found in 1879 by Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola and his young daughter María, it was the first Palaeolithic cave art recognised as such. The cave is closed to protect the paintings; this is a scan of the full-size replica in the Deutsches Museum in Munich, hung overhead as the original is, so look up.
facts: The painters used the bulges of the ceiling for the bodies of the bison, so the animals stand out in relief in raking light.
Sautuola's claim that the paintings were prehistoric was dismissed as a forgery; he died in 1888, fourteen years before the experts conceded he was right.
The ceiling is about 18 by 9 metres; the Deutsches Museum's replica was made in 1962 and is itself now a historic object.

artworks.title: Clovis point (Clovis lanceolate spear point)

location.name: Chapel Hill, North Carolina
location.institution: Research Laboratories of Archaeology, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill (North Carolina Archaeological Collection)

artworks.medium: Knapped metavolcanic stone, fluted lanceolate projectile point
artworks.description: Clovis points are the fluted, lance-shaped spear tips of the Clovis culture, the earliest widespread tool tradition in the Americas. A shallow channel, or flute, struck from the base on each face let the point be seated in a split wooden or bone shaft. This example, knapped from metavolcanic stone, was found in the Piedmont of North Carolina and donated to the University of North Carolina, whose archaeology laboratory made the scan.
facts: Clovis points are named after Clovis, New Mexico, where the first examples were found in 1929 by Ridgely Whiteman.
All known Clovis points date to roughly 13,400–12,700 years ago, often in association with mammoth and other Ice Age animal remains.
Finished points were fluted on both faces so they could be hafted; the technique was passed between knappers across the continent.

artworks.title: Nordeste tradition figures, Serra da Capivara

creators.name: Unknown painters of the Nordeste tradition

artworks.medium: red ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A red deer-like animal and small human figures on a sandstone shelter in the Serra da Capivara, where more than a thousand painted shelters record hunting, dancing and sex in the lively Nordeste style. The park is at the centre of the argument over when people reached the Americas: its excavator Niède Guidon claims hearths over 30,000 years old, far older than most archaeologists accept.
facts: Serra da Capivara holds the largest concentration of rock art in the Americas.
The Nordeste tradition is usually dated between about 12,000 and 6,000 years ago.
Capivara means capybara, the park's name animal.

artworks.title: Rock Shelter 8, Bhimbetka

creators.name: Unknown Mesolithic painters of central India

artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A frieze of red animals and small hunters inside one of the sandstone shelters at Bhimbetka, south of Bhopal, where some 750 shelters were painted over and over from the Mesolithic to the medieval period. The oldest figures, like these, are red; later ones are white and show riders, elephants and battles.
facts: The shelters were noticed by the archaeologist V. S. Wakankar from a train window in 1957.
Stone tools in the shelters go back 100,000 years, long before the paintings.
Bhimbetka was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2003.

artworks.title: Cueva de las Manos
artworks.medium: mineral pigment blown through bone pipes
artworks.description: Hundreds of hands stencilled in red, white, black and ochre on the wall of a cave above the Río Pinturas in Patagonia. The painters held a hand to the rock and blew pigment over it through a bone pipe; most are left hands, so the pipe was held in the right. Guanaco hunts and geometric patterns were painted around them over several thousand years.
facts: The oldest layer has been dated to around 9,300 years ago.
Of about 830 hands, only 31 are right hands.
The cave was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1999.

artworks.title: Pastoral figures, Tanzoumaitak, Tassili n'Ajjer

creators.name: Unknown painters of the Saharan Pastoral period

artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: Running and dancing figures in ochre on a sandstone shelter at Tanzoumaitak, on the Tassili n'Ajjer plateau in the Algerian Sahara. When they were painted the Sahara was green: the plateau's 15,000 paintings and engravings show cattle herds, giraffes, hippos and swimmers where there is now only rock and sand.
facts: Henri Lhote's expeditions in the 1950s, guided by the Tuareg Jebrine ag Mohamed, copied thousands of the paintings and made the site famous.
The Round Head period, the plateau's oldest painted style, may go back 10,000 years; the Pastoral period that follows is the richest.
Tassili n'Ajjer was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1982.

artworks.title: Cattle, Laas Geel

creators.name: Unknown Neolithic painters of the Horn of Africa

artworks.medium: ochre, white and black pigment on granite
artworks.description: Long-horned cows with decorated necks and ceremonial collars, painted in red, white and black on the ceiling of a granite shelter at Laas Geel, outside Hargeisa. The cows are shown with their udders and without legs below the knee, as if seen from the front, and small human figures stand beneath them with their arms raised. The site is among the best preserved rock art in Africa.
facts: Local herders had always known the shelters; a French team recorded them for archaeology in 2002.
There are about twenty painted shelters on the granite outcrop.
Laas Geel means 'the camels' waterhole' in Somali.

artworks.title: Proto-cuneiform tablet: account of barley distribution

madeIn.name: Southern Mesopotamia (find-spot unrecorded; placed at Uruk)

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

artworks.medium: Clay, impressed with a stylus and a cylinder seal
artworks.description: A small clay tablet recording the distribution of barley in the pictographic proto-cuneiform script, the earliest stage of writing in Mesopotamia. Numerical notations are pressed into the clay with the round end of a stylus beside signs for the commodity and its recipients. The reverse and edges were rolled with a cylinder seal showing a man with hunting dogs and boars.
facts: Dated by the Met to about 3100-2900 BCE, the Jemdet Nasr period, when writing was still largely pictographic.
The tablet measures 5.4 by 6 by 4.1 cm and entered the Met in 1988 as a Raymond and Beverly Sackler gift purchase.
Proto-cuneiform tablets are almost all administrative records, listing goods, rations and labour rather than language as speech.

artworks.title: Great Pyramid of Giza
artworks.medium: Limestone masonry, shown as a shape at true size
artworks.description: The tomb of the pharaoh Khufu, raised on the Giza plateau over about twenty years around 2560 BCE: some 2.3 million blocks of limestone, the largest weighing tens of tonnes, laid in 210 courses to a height of 146.6 metres on a base 230 metres square, level to within a few centimetres and aligned to true north within a twentieth of a degree. It was the tallest structure made by people for nearly four thousand years, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire, and it is the one wonder of the ancient world still standing. No scan of it may be freely used, and a photograph cannot say how big it is, so it stands here as a plain shape at its true size, six hundred metres off the lane. Walk out to it, or look up from its foot.
facts: Its base covers 5.3 hectares; its volume is about 2.6 million cubic metres.
The top 8 metres and the polished white casing are gone; it stands 138.5 m today.
The workforce was paid and fed, not enslaved: their bakeries, barracks and tombs lie beside it.
Its four sides face the cardinal directions to within 0.05 degrees.

artworks.title: Stonehenge (reconstruction)

date.label: c. 2500 BCE (sarsen circle; the earthwork c. 3000 BCE)

artworks.medium: Sarsen sandstone trilithons and circle, with bluestones from Wales, set in a circular earthwork
artworks.description: Walk in among the stones. Around 2500 BCE, people with no metal, no wheel and no writing dragged sarsen blocks of up to 30 tonnes some 25 km across Salisbury Plain, shaped them with stone hammers, and raised them into a ring of thirty uprights capped by a continuous lintel, with five great trilithons in a horseshoe inside, all aligned so that the midsummer sun rises along its axis. The smaller bluestones had come 250 km from the hills of west Wales, centuries earlier. Nobody knows what the builders meant by it: a temple, a calendar, a place of the dead, a place of healing. This is an artist's model of the monument as it stands today, placed so you can walk through the circle; the fallen and missing stones are as they are.
facts: The largest trilithon stood 7.3 m above ground and weighed about 50 tonnes; the lintels are held by mortise-and-tenon joints, carpentry in stone.
The bluestones were quarried in the Preseli Hills of Pembrokeshire, and the giant Altar Stone, a 2024 study found, came from the far north-east of Scotland.
The whole monument was built and rebuilt over about 1,500 years, from the first ditch around 3000 BCE to the last rearrangement around 1600 BCE.

artworks.title: Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro
artworks.medium: Bronze, lost-wax cast
artworks.description: A bronze figure of a girl, only 10.5 centimetres tall, found in 1926 in a house in the ruined city of Mohenjo-daro on the Indus, in what is now Pakistan. She stands with her weight on one leg, right hand on her hip, head tilted back, her left arm stacked with bangles from wrist to shoulder; John Marshall, who dug the city, thought she was beating time to music, hence her name. She was cast by the lost-wax process some 4,500 years ago, which makes her one of the earliest bronze figures in the world and the oldest known example of the technique in South Asia, a method Indian metalworkers would still be using for the Chola Natarajas four thousand years later. The Indus civilisation built planned brick cities with drains and baths while most of the world lived in villages, and its script is still unread; this small, confident figure is one of the few faces it left us. At Partition in 1947 the finds from Mohenjo-daro were divided between the two new countries, and she came to Delhi.
facts: Excavated by Ernest Mackay in the 'HR area' of Mohenjo-daro in 1926.
10.5 cm high and 5 cm wide; she wears 24 or 25 bangles on her left arm and four on her right.
One of the earliest lost-wax bronze castings known anywhere.
Mortimer Wheeler called her his favourite statuette: 'There's nothing like her, I think, in the world.'

artworks.title: Nebra sky disc
artworks.medium: Bronze disc with gold inlays
artworks.description: A bronze disc with a blue-green patina inlaid with gold symbols: a full sun or moon, a crescent, a cluster of seven stars read as the Pleiades, two horizon arcs marking the solstice sunrise and sunset, and a boat. Buried on the Mittelberg near Nebra with swords, axes and arm spirals, it is the oldest known concrete depiction of the night sky.
facts: Found in 1999 by two unlicensed metal-detectorists and recovered by police in a sting in Basel in 2002.
About 30 cm across and 2.2 kg; 38 to 40 holes were punched around the rim before burial.
Added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Register in 2013.

artworks.title: Neck-amphora with a wedding procession, by Exekias

location.name: The Metropolitan Museum of Art
location.institution: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

artworks.medium: Terracotta, black-figure
artworks.description: Lidded neck-amphora attributed to Exekias, the leading Athenian black-figure potter-painter of the mid sixth century BC. On the body a couple ride in a four-horse chariot in a procession, accompanied by a kithara player and a foot soldier, beneath a band of palmettes and lotus on the neck. Exekias' work is marked by precise incision and dignified, static compositions; the lid with its bud-shaped knob survives with the vase.
facts: Exekias was active in Athens between roughly 545 and 530 BC and worked as both potter and painter.
The vase stands 47 cm high and 24.8 cm in diameter and is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art (Rogers Fund, 1917).

creators.role: author of the Elements; the theorem is older

artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: In a right triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the squares on the other two sides. The relation was known to Babylonian scribes more than a thousand years before Pythagoras, and the proof that closes Book I of Euclid's Elements, written in Alexandria around 300 BCE, is the form in which the world learned it: Euclid's textbook stayed in use for over two thousand years. It is the first equation most people ever meet, and the one that turns geometry into arithmetic.
facts: The Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322, from about 1800 BCE, lists whole-number triples such as 3, 4, 5 that satisfy the relation.
Pythagoras, who lived around 570 to 495 BCE, left no writings; the theorem was attached to his name by later Greek tradition.
Hundreds of proofs are known, including one published in 1876 by James Garfield, five years before he became president of the United States.

artworks.title: Tamil-Brahmi inscription at Arittapatti

location.name: Arittapatti, Madurai district
location.institution: Archaeological Survey of India protected site (in situ)

artworks.medium: Letters chiselled into a granite rock shelter
artworks.description: These letters, chiselled into the brow of a granite rock shelter at Arittapatti near Madurai, are among the earliest writing in the Tamil language. They are in Tamil-Brahmi (தமிழி, Tamili), a southern adaptation of the Brahmi script of Ashoka's edicts, with extra letters invented for the Tamil sounds ழ, ள, ற and ன that northern Brahmi could not write. Inscriptions like this one, found in dozens of caves around Madurai, record gifts of rock shelters and stone beds to Jain monks who lived on the hills during the Sangam age, and they name the donors, merchants, village headmen and the kings of the Pandya country. The script is dated to between the third century BCE and the first century CE, which makes it the oldest evidence of a written literary language in South India and the ancestor of the Tamil alphabet used today. Nearby Mangulam has the oldest group of all, naming the Pandya king Nedunchezhiyan, and the Keezhadi excavations have since found the same script scratched on everyday pottery.
facts: Tamil-Brahmi adds letters for sounds that exist in Tamil but not in the Prakrit of the Ashokan edicts, which is how scholars identified it as Tamil in 1924.
The inscription was first published by K. V. Raman and Y. Subbarayalu in 1971.
The same hill has a Jain tirthankara relief with a much later Vatteluttu inscription and a 7th-century rock-cut Shiva temple.
Iravatham Mahadevan's corpus of 1966-2003 established the readings of nearly a hundred such cave inscriptions in Tamil Nadu.

artworks.title: Euclid's Elements: the Oxyrhynchus papyrus with the diagram (P.Oxy. I 29)

date.label: c. 75-125 CE (Penn Museum: 3rd-4th century CE); text composed c. 300 BCE

location.name: Philadelphia
location.institution: Penn Museum (University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology)

artworks.medium: Ink on papyrus
artworks.description: A scrap of papyrus the size of a postcard, dug out of the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus in Egypt by Grenfell and Hunt in 1896-97, carrying the oldest surviving diagram from Euclid's Elements. The nine lines of Greek state Proposition 5 of Book II: if a straight line is cut into equal and unequal parts, the rectangle contained by the unequal parts, together with the square on the line between the points of section, equals the square on the half. The little figure at the lower right is the rectangle and squares that prove it; in modern notation it is the identity ab + ((a+b)/2 - b)² = ((a+b)/2)². Euclid compiled the Elements in Alexandria around 300 BCE, and it was copied for two thousand years as the model of what a proof should be. This page was written some four centuries after his death, perhaps for a student, and about eight centuries before the oldest complete manuscript of the Elements, which was made in 888.
facts: Written on one side only, in sloping capitals with a few spelling slips, probably from a roll or a loose sheet.
The Elements ran to thirteen books and was printed in more editions than any book but the Bible.
Grenfell and Hunt's Oxyrhynchus finds amount to about half a million papyrus fragments, most still unpublished.
The fragment came to Philadelphia in 1901 as thanks for the university's support of the Egypt Exploration Fund.

artworks.title: The Pantheon, Rome (interior)

creators.name: Unknown architect, for the emperor Hadrian

location.name: Rome
location.institution: Basilica of St Mary and the Martyrs (the Pantheon)

artworks.medium: Rotunda of brick-faced Roman concrete under an unreinforced concrete dome, with a granite-columned portico
artworks.description: Walk in. The Pantheon's rotunda is a perfect sphere's worth of space, 43.3 m across and 43.3 m high, under the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built, open to the sky through a 9 m oculus that is its only window. Hadrian had it built around 113 to 126 CE on the site of Agrippa's temple of 27 BCE, whose name still runs across the portico, and it has stood in continuous use since, as a temple to all the gods and, from 609, as a church. Its builders lightened the concrete with pumice toward the top, thinned the dome from 6.4 m at the base to 1.2 m at the oculus, and sank the coffers to save weight. Nobody surpassed the span for thirteen hundred years. This is a photogrammetry scan of the interior; the floor is the scanner's reconstruction.
facts: The dome is still, after nineteen centuries, the world's largest made of unreinforced concrete; Brunelleschi studied it before building Florence's.
The oculus is open to the weather. Rain falls on the floor, which slopes to drains, and the circle of sunlight walks across the coffers through the day.
Raphael is buried here, at his own request, with the epitaph 'Here lies Raphael, by whom Nature feared to be outdone while he lived, and when he died, feared she too would die.'

artworks.title: Iron Pillar of Delhi
artworks.medium: Forge-welded wrought iron
artworks.description: A column of solid wrought iron 7.21 metres tall, 41 centimetres across and over six tonnes in weight, standing in the courtyard of the Qutb complex in Delhi. A Sanskrit inscription in Gupta script says it was raised as a standard of Vishnu by a king called Chandra, almost certainly Chandragupta II, who reigned from about 375 to 415 CE; it was probably first set up at Udayagiri in central India and moved to Delhi in the eleventh century, two hundred years before the Qutb Minar was built beside it. No one else in the world could make a single iron object this large for another thousand years: it was built up by forge-welding many lumps of hot iron, hammered together by hand. Most famously, it has stood in the open for sixteen centuries without rusting. The reason is the metal itself: a high phosphorus content, a product of the ancient Indian smelting process, lets a thin protective film of iron hydrogen phosphate form on the surface and seal it. Scientists did not understand this until the 1990s.
facts: 7.21 m tall including 1.12 m below ground; 41 cm in diameter at the base; estimated weight over six tonnes.
The oldest inscription names King Chandra and dedicates the pillar to Vishnu; it covers about 65 by 27 cm of the surface.
Its rust resistance comes from phosphorus in the iron, which forms a protective crystalline layer (misawite).
Moved to Delhi by the Tomar king Anangpal II in the 11th century, long before the mosque now around it.

artworks.title: Bodhisattva Padmapani, Cave 1, Ajanta
artworks.medium: Tempera on mud-and-lime plaster over rock
artworks.description: The Bodhisattva Padmapani, 'he who holds the lotus', painted beside the shrine door of Cave 1 at Ajanta in the last decades of the fifth century. He stands over life size, his body swaying in a gentle curve, a blue lotus in his right hand, eyes half closed, surrounded by a crowd of smaller figures: attendants, a dark-skinned guard, musicians and animals. Ajanta is a horseshoe of thirty Buddhist monasteries and prayer halls cut into a cliff above a river gorge in the Deccan. The earliest date from the second century BCE; the great painted caves, including this one, were made in a single burst of patronage under the Vakataka king Harisena around 460 to 480 CE, then abandoned and forgotten in the jungle until a British hunting party found them in 1819. The paintings are tempera on a thin plaster of mud, lime and rice husk, and are the oldest surviving body of Indian painting. Padmapani is the single most reproduced image from them and has shaped how Indian art is pictured ever since.
facts: Cave 1 was probably sponsored by the Vakataka emperor Harisena and was never formally consecrated: there is no lamp-soot on the shrine image.
Padmapani and his pair Vajrapani flank the entrance to the Buddha shrine on the rear wall; both are over life size.
The pigments are earth colours plus lapis lazuli blue imported from Afghanistan.
The caves were lost to the forest for roughly a thousand years before their rediscovery in 1819.

artworks.medium: ochre on sandstone
artworks.description: A long-necked turtle painted in the X-ray style of western Arnhem Land, with its backbone and organs drawn inside the outline. The X-ray convention appears in Kakadu's galleries over the last two or three thousand years, at the end of a painting tradition that goes back more than 20,000 years, and shows the food animals of the wetlands: barramundi, catfish, goannas, wallabies and turtles.
facts: Kakadu's rock art tradition is one of the longest continuous ones in the world, and the Bininj and Mungguy custodians still know the stories behind many paintings.
X-ray paintings show what you learn by butchering the animal: which parts are eaten and how.
Kakadu was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1981 for both its nature and its culture.

artworks.title: Tirukkural: palm-leaf manuscript with Parimelalhagar's commentary

date.label: c. 450–500 CE (text); this copy 19th century or earlier

artworks.medium: Ink-rubbed incised script on dried palm leaf
artworks.description: A single leaf of a palm-leaf manuscript of the Tirukkural (திருக்குறள்), the most loved book in the Tamil language. The Kural is a collection of 1,330 couplets, each of just seven words, on virtue, wealth and love, written by the poet Valluvar (திருவள்ளுவர்) around the fifth century CE, perhaps earlier. This leaf carries the first two couplets, beginning 'As the letter A is the first of all letters, so the primal God is first in the world', with the commentary of the thirteenth-century scholar Parimelalhagar written between the lines of verse. For over a thousand years the text survived only this way: letters scratched with a stylus into strips of dried palmyra leaf, the grooves rubbed with soot or lamp-black, the leaves strung together and recopied every century or two before they crumbled. The Kural was the first book printed in Tamil, in 1812, from blocks cut to imitate leaves like this one. It is quoted in Tamil homes, courts and parliaments to this day.
facts: 1,330 couplets in 133 chapters of ten; every couplet has exactly seven words in the kural metre.
Nothing certain is known about the author; the honorific Thiruvalluvar means 'the revered Valluvar'.
Dated by linguists to about 450–500 CE; traditional accounts place it earlier, in the Sangam age.
Translated into more than forty languages; the first English selection appeared in 1794.

artworks.title: Brahmagupta's rules for zero
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Zero as a number, with rules for doing arithmetic on it. Counting systems had used an empty place for centuries, but in 628 CE Brahmagupta, writing the Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta in Bhinmal in what is now Rajasthan, was the first to treat śūnya, zero, as a number in its own right: adding it changes nothing, a number less itself is zero, anything times zero is zero. In the same chapter he gave the rules for negative numbers, which he called debts, and for positives, fortunes. Together with the place-value numerals India had already invented, this is the arithmetic the whole world now uses, carried west through Baghdad in the ninth century and into Europe as 'Arabic' numerals.
facts: Brahmagupta's one wrong rule was that zero divided by zero is zero; division by zero stayed a puzzle for a thousand years.
The Bakhshali manuscript, a birch-bark text from near Peshawar, carries a dot for zero that radiocarbon dating in 2017 placed in the third or fourth century, the oldest known.
Al-Khwarizmi's ninth-century treatise on the Indian numerals brought the system to the Islamic world; Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 brought it to Europe.

artworks.title: Descent of the Ganges (Arjuna's Penance), Mamallapuram

location.name: Mamallapuram
location.institution: Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram (in situ)

artworks.medium: Relief carved into two granite boulders
artworks.description: Carved across two granite boulders at Mamallapuram on the Coromandel coast, this is the largest bas-relief in the world: 29 metres wide and 13 metres high, with more than a hundred figures of gods, people and animals. Tamils call it Arjunan Tapasu (அர்ச்சுனன் தபசு), Arjuna's Penance, after the gaunt figure standing on one leg beside the central cleft; the other reading is that he is Bhagiratha, whose austerities brought the river Ganges down from heaven to earth. The cleft between the boulders, which once carried real water from a tank above, stands for the river, and serpent-deities (nagas) rise in it. To its right walks a family of life-size elephants, among the most admired animal sculptures in India. The relief was cut in the mid-seventh century under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla, the great wrestler, from whom the town takes its name. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Group of Monuments at Mahabalipuram.
facts: At about 29 by 13 metres it is the largest open-air rock relief in the world.
A cistern above the cleft once released water down the channel so that the Ganges actually flowed between the carved nagas.
The elephants are carved at life size; a sly cat 'doing penance' among mice beneath them is a famous joke in stone.
An unfinished copy of the same composition stands a few hundred metres away, abandoned by the Pallava carvers.

artworks.medium: ochre, blood and egg binder on sandstone
artworks.description: An eland in shaded red and white on a sandstone shelter in the Drakensberg, painted by the San with a fine brush and a polychrome technique that modelled the animal's bulk. The eland is the animal that appears most often in San painting; it was the creature of greatest spiritual power, and the trance dance of the healers drew on its potency.
facts: The Drakensberg holds some 35,000 to 40,000 painted images in over 600 shelters.
Most of the paintings are less than 2,000 years old and some show horses and guns from the 1800s.
The park was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2000.

artworks.movement: Northern Song monumental landscape (Northern Landscape style)
artworks.medium: Hanging scroll, ink and light colour on silk
artworks.description: A single cliff face rises almost the full height of the silk, with a thread of waterfall at its right and a mule train and travellers reduced to specks along the stream at its foot. Fan Kuan, a recluse who studied the mountains of Shaanxi directly, painted it around 1000; it is the defining work of Northern Song monumental landscape. The painter's signature, hidden among the foliage at lower right, was only rediscovered in 1958.

Fan Kuan's half-hidden signature in the leaves at the lower right was rediscovered in 1958.
The Ming painter-critic Dong Qichang is said to have called it the finest painting of the Song dynasty.

artworks.title: Brihadisvara Temple, Thanjavur
artworks.medium: Granite masonry
artworks.description: The Brihadisvara Temple, known to Tamils as Thanjai Periya Kovil (தஞ்சைப் பெரிய கோவில், the Big Temple of Thanjavur) and to its builder as Rajarajesvaram, was raised between 1003 and 1010 by the Chola emperor Rajaraja I, in the capital of an empire that then ruled most of South India and Sri Lanka. Its vimana, the pyramidal tower over the sanctum, rises about 66 metres from a square base 30 metres on a side, in sixteen storeys of carved granite: the tallest building in India for centuries, and still one of the tallest temple towers in the world. The sanctum holds a monolithic linga nearly nine metres high. The granite was quarried far away, since there is none near Thanjavur, and tradition says the eighty-tonne capstone was dragged up a ramp several kilometres long. Long inscriptions on the base record the dancers, musicians, accountants and lamp-lighters the temple employed, and the gifts of gold and villages that paid for them. It has been in continuous worship for a thousand years and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
facts: Built in about seven years and consecrated in 1010 CE; the thousandth anniversary was celebrated in 2010.
The vimana is about 66 m tall on a 30 m square base; the sanctum's linga alone is 8.7 m high.
Chola inscriptions carved around the plinth name the temple's 400 dancers and list its endowments village by village.
The architect is named in inscriptions as Kunjara Mallan Raja Raja Perunthachan.

contributed.note: The vimana seen straight on from the courtyard, in daylight, no one but a few small figures at the plinth: a Commons Quality Image, taken 15 August 2016 (Sony ILCA-77M2, Sigma 18-35 mm). artworks.title: Nataraja, Shiva as the Lord of Dance
artworks.medium: Bronze (copper alloy), lost-wax cast
artworks.description: Shiva as Nataraja, the Lord of Dance (Tamil: நடராஜர், Nataraja; also ஆடவல்லான், Adavallan), cast in bronze in Tamil Nadu in the eleventh century, at the height of the Chola empire. The god dances inside a ring of fire. His upper right hand beats a small drum, the sound that begins creation; his upper left holds the flame that will end it. The lower right hand is raised in the gesture that says 'do not fear', and the lower left points to the lifted foot, where release is found. The other foot presses down on Apasmara, the dwarf of ignorance. The whole figure, with its halo and lotus base, stands over a metre tall and was made by the lost-wax method, in which a wax model is coated in clay, melted out and replaced with molten metal, so each bronze is unique. Images like this were carried in procession at temple festivals, dressed and garlanded. The Nataraja is the most famous form of South Indian art, and the one that Tamil people most readily recognise as their own.
facts: Made in Tamil Nadu under the Chola dynasty, whose bronze-casters produced the finest metal sculpture in India between the 9th and 13th centuries.
Cast by the lost-wax process, so the mould was destroyed and every Chola bronze is a one-off.
The Cleveland Museum of Art scanned the bronze itself and released the model under CC0; it measures 113 by 102 by 30 cm with its ring of fire.
A Nataraja of this type stands outside CERN in Geneva, given by India in 2004 as an image of the cosmic dance of matter.

artworks.title: A courtyard of the Nasrid palaces, the Alhambra

creators.name: Nasrid court workshops, for Yusuf I and Muhammad V

date.label: 14th century, under Yusuf I and Muhammad V

location.name: Granada
location.institution: Patronato de la Alhambra y Generalife (in situ)

artworks.medium: Brick, lime plaster carved in relief, glazed tile and carved wood
artworks.description: Walk in. The Alhambra is the palace city of the Nasrid emirs of Granada, the last Muslim state in Spain, and its palaces of the fourteenth century are the finest thing Islamic Spain left behind: courtyards of water and shade, walls of carved plaster that dissolve into pattern, ceilings of wooden geometry and muqarnas that hang like honeycomb. Nothing in them is heavy; the materials are brick and plaster and tile, cheap stuff, and the whole art is in the surface and the proportion. This is one of the first courtyards on the way in, scanned by a visitor with a camera; stand in it and look at the facade with its carved eave and the gallery of arches above the door. The scan has holes and a rough patch over one corner, as scans do. The rest is as it stands in Granada.
facts: The Nasrids ruled Granada from 1238 until Ferdinand and Isabella took the city on 2 January 1492.
The plaster was carved wet, in panels, and painted; traces of blue and red survive in the recesses.
Inscriptions on the walls repeat the Nasrid motto, 'There is no victor but God', hundreds of times.
Washington Irving lived in the half-ruined palace in 1829 and wrote the book that brought the world to it.

contributed.note: Photogrammetry of the first courtyard on the visitor's way through the Nasrid palaces ('Primer Patio'), by Sketchfab user EternalEchoesVR, CC BY 4.0 (license.txt: author EternalEchoesVR, license type CC-BY-4.0). The plan sits about 20 degrees off the axes in the file; rotated back. The decorated two-storey facade with the large arched portal and the gallery of three arches faces into the courtyard from its -Z end; the +Z end is a low six-arch arcade, which is the way in. artworks.title: Madhava's series for π
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: An infinite sum for π, and the first steps of calculus, from Kerala around 1400. Madhava of Sangamagrama found that the odd fractions, added and subtracted in turn, close in on a quarter of π, and he found the same kind of endless series for the sine and cosine; he even worked out correction terms that gave π to eleven decimal places. His own writings are lost, but his school kept them, in Sanskrit and in Malayalam verse, in Nilakantha's Tantrasangraha of 1501 and Jyeshthadeva's Yuktibhāṣā of about 1530. Europe reached the same series through Gregory in 1671 and Leibniz in 1674, nearly three centuries later.
facts: The series converges painfully slowly, a few hundred terms for two decimal places; Madhava's correction terms fixed that, which is why his school had π to eleven places.
The Yuktibhāṣā, written in Malayalam, gives proofs as well as results, and is counted among the first texts of calculus anywhere.
The Kerala school ran for two centuries, from Madhava to Achyuta Pisharati around 1600, in a cluster of villages along the Nila river.

contributed.note: Typeset by 20watts from the TeX in the record with MathJax, with a figure drawn for this museum; the rendering is CC0, the equation itself is not subject to copyright.

artworks.title: Gutenberg Bible, first page of Genesis (Berlin vellum copy)
artworks.medium: Letterpress printing in Textura type on vellum, with hand-painted initial, border and rubrication
artworks.description: 'In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth': the opening of Genesis in the first substantial book printed in Europe with movable metal type. Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith's son from Mainz, worked out how to cast thousands of identical letters in a hand mould, how to mix an oil-based ink that would stick to metal, and how to adapt a wine press to print a sheet. Around 1454 and 1455 his workshop printed about 180 copies of the Latin Bible, some on paper and some, like this one, on calfskin, in two volumes of 1,286 pages with two columns of 42 lines each. Only the black text came off the press; the great initial, the border with its birds and peacock, the red headings and the coloured capitals were painted in afterwards by hand, so that no two copies look alike. The whole enterprise was financed by a loan from Johann Fust, who foreclosed before the Bibles were sold. Forty-nine copies survive; this page is from the illuminated vellum copy in Berlin.
facts: Printed in a Textura typeface of some 290 different sorts, including ligatures and abbreviations, to imitate a scribe's hand.
A scribe took about three years to copy a Bible; Gutenberg's press produced the whole edition in about two.
Twenty-one complete copies survive; the Berlin copy is one of about a dozen printed on vellum.
Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, the future Pope Pius II, saw sheets at Frankfurt in October 1454 and reported that they could be read without spectacles.

artworks.title: The Last Supper

location.name: Milan
location.institution: Refectory of the Convent of Santa Maria delle Grazie

artworks.medium: tempera on gesso, pitch and mastic
artworks.description: Painted on the north wall of the refectory of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan, the mural shows the moment Jesus tells the apostles that one of them will betray him. Leonardo abandoned true fresco for an experimental tempera-on-dry-wall technique, which let him work slowly but began to deteriorate within decades.
facts: The apostles are arranged in four groups of three, reacting in waves to Jesus's announcement.
The perspective lines converge on Jesus's right temple.
A door was cut through the bottom of the mural in 1652, removing Jesus's feet.
The refectory survived an Allied bomb in 1943 that destroyed the roof and one wall; the mural had been sandbagged.

artworks.title: Newton's law of universal gravitation
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Every mass attracts every other with a force proportional to the product of the masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Newton set it out in the Principia, published in London on 5 July 1687, and showed that the same rule governs a falling apple, the Moon's orbit, the planets and the tides. It was the first law to hold for the whole universe at once, and it stood unchallenged for 228 years, until Einstein's field equations further along this lane.
facts: Newton wrote the Principia in about eighteen months after Edmond Halley visited him in Cambridge in 1684 to ask what orbit an inverse-square force would produce.
The constant G was first measured in 1798, by Henry Cavendish, with a torsion balance in a shed; the symbol G came into use only in the 1890s.
Newton refused to explain what gravity is: 'Hypotheses non fingo', I frame no hypotheses, he wrote in the second edition.

artworks.title: Newton, Principia Mathematica, title page of the first edition

location.name: Strasbourg
location.institution: Université de Strasbourg, Service commun de la documentation

artworks.medium: Letterpress printing on paper, quarto
artworks.description: The title page of the book that gave physics its laws. Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica, 'Mathematical Principles of Natural Philosophy', sets out Newton's three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation, and uses them to derive Kepler's planetary orbits, the tides, the shape of the Earth, the precession of the equinoxes and the paths of comets, all from one inverse-square force. The page records how it came to be printed: 'Imprimatur, S. Pepys, Reg. Soc. Præses, Julii 5. 1686', the licence of the Royal Society under its president Samuel Pepys, and 'Jussu Societatis Regiæ ac Typis Josephi Streater', printed by Joseph Streater at the Society's order. In fact the Society had spent its money on a history of fishes, and the astronomer Edmond Halley, who had prodded Newton into writing the book, paid for the printing himself. Newton is named as Lucasian Professor at Trinity College, Cambridge. Only a few hundred copies were printed, in Latin, and they sold for about nine shillings.
facts: Newton wrote the three books in about eighteen months, between 1685 and 1686.
Halley's prompt was a question in 1684: what orbit does an inverse-square force give? Newton answered 'an ellipse', and had already proved it.
Second and third editions followed in 1713 and 1726; Newton's own annotated first edition survives at Trinity College.
The first English translation, by Andrew Motte, appeared in 1729, two years after Newton's death.

artworks.title: Brandenburg Concerto No. 3
artworks.medium: Concerto for three violins, three violas, three cellos and continuo; autograph dedication score, ink on paper
artworks.description: In March 1721 Johann Sebastian Bach, then Kapellmeister to the small court of Anhalt-Köthen, sent a beautifully copied set of six concertos to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg, with a flattering French dedication. The margrave seems never to have had them played; the score sat in his library and was valued at a few groschen when he died. Today the six are the most celebrated orchestral works of the Baroque. The third concerto, in G major, is written for three violins, three violas, three cellos and continuo, and Bach treats the nine string parts as a single shifting texture, passing figures between the groups in rapid conversation. The page shown here is Bach's own title page from the dedication score, now in the Berlin State Library. The visitor hears the first movement, played by the Advent Chamber Orchestra in a live concert recording from December 2006, released under a Creative Commons licence.
facts: The dedication is dated 24 March 1721; the concertos themselves were probably composed over the preceding years at Köthen and Weimar.
The third concerto has no full slow movement, only two chords linking the two fast movements, which players often expand with a short improvised cadenza.
The dedication score survived in the Berlin Royal Library and is now Am.B. 78 at the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin.

artworks.title: The Four Seasons: Spring

location.name: Paris
location.institution: Bibliothèque nationale de France (first-edition part-book shown)

artworks.medium: Violin concerto in E major, RV 269, with strings and continuo; engraved first edition
artworks.description: Antonio Vivaldi, a Venetian priest who taught the violin at the Ospedale della Pietà, an orphanage famous for its girls' orchestra, published twelve concertos in Amsterdam in 1725 under the title 'The Contest of Harmony and Invention'. The first four are the Four Seasons, and each is prefaced by a sonnet, probably by Vivaldi himself, whose lines are printed in the parts at the moments they describe. 'Spring' opens with birdsong traded between three violins, a murmuring brook, a thunderstorm, and then a sleeping goatherd, a barking dog in the violas, and a rustic bagpipe dance. It is among the earliest and most vivid examples of music telling a story, and today the most performed Baroque work of all. The sheet shown is the title page of the 1725 Le Cène edition from the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The visitor hears the first movement, played by John Harrison with the Wichita State University Chamber Players in a live recording from 2000, released under a Creative Commons licence.
facts: The concertos were dedicated to the Bohemian count Wenzel von Morzin, and had probably been circulating in manuscript for several years before publication.
Each season carries a sonnet, with letters in the score linking lines of verse to passages of music, such as 'the barking dog' for the viola in the Largo.
Vivaldi's reputation collapsed after his death in 1741 and the Four Seasons were almost unknown until the 1940s, when the first recordings appeared.

artworks.title: Euler's identity
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Five constants from five corners of mathematics, e from growth, i from the square roots of negatives, π from circles, and 1 and 0, bound in one line. It is the special case at x = π of Euler's formula e^{ix} = cos x + i sin x, which Euler published in 1748 in his Introductio in analysin infinitorum, written while he led the mathematics class of the Berlin Academy. Mathematicians have voted it the most beautiful theorem in the subject more than once.
facts: Euler was the most prolific mathematician in history, with some 850 works; he kept writing after going blind in 1771, dictating to assistants.
Richard Feynman called the underlying formula 'our jewel' and 'the most remarkable formula in mathematics'.
Euler introduced much of the notation on this sheet: e for the base of natural logarithms, i for the square root of minus one, and the use of π.

artworks.title: Bayes' theorem
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: How to update a belief when evidence arrives: the probability of a hypothesis given the data is the probability of the data given the hypothesis, times the prior, divided by the probability of the data. Thomas Bayes, a Presbyterian minister in Tunbridge Wells, worked it out and never published it; his friend Richard Price found the essay among his papers after his death and read it to the Royal Society on 23 December 1763. It is the equation every learning machine, and arguably every 20-watt brain, runs on.
facts: Pierre-Simon Laplace rediscovered the rule independently in 1774 and gave it the general form used today.
Alan Turing's team at Bletchley Park used Bayesian reasoning to break Enigma; the bombe drums a few rows back are the hardware.
Bayes' original essay solved one problem: given the outcomes of some trials, what is the chance of success on the next?

artworks.description: Mozart entered this serenade for strings in his personal catalogue on 10 August 1787 in Vienna, while he was in the middle of composing the opera Don Giovanni. He called it simply 'Eine kleine Nacht Musik', a little night music, meaning a short serenade of the kind played outdoors at evening entertainments. Nobody knows who commissioned it or when it was first played, and the work was not published until 1827, long after his death. Its opening fanfare, rising through a G major chord, has since become one of the most recognised phrases in Western music. The page shown is the first leaf of Mozart's own manuscript, written quickly and almost without corrections. The visitor hears the first movement, Allegro, in a recording by the Advent Chamber Orchestra from its 2005-06 season, released under a Creative Commons licence.
facts: Mozart's catalogue lists five movements; the second, a minuet, is lost, so the serenade is almost always heard in four.
The manuscript was sold by Mozart's widow Constanze to the publisher Johann Anton André in 1799, and was first printed in 1827.
The title in Mozart's catalogue is 'Eine kleine Nacht Musik, bestehend in einem Allegro, Menuett und Trio, Romance, Menuett und Trio, und Finale'.

artworks.title: Symphony No. 5 in C minor

date.label: 22 December 1808 (premiere, Theater an der Wien); composed 1804-1808

artworks.medium: Symphony for orchestra; autograph score, ink on paper
artworks.description: Beethoven worked on his Fifth Symphony between 1804 and 1808, in the years when his deafness was becoming impossible to hide. It was first played on 22 December 1808 at the Theater an der Wien in Vienna, in a freezing hall, as part of a four-hour concert of his new music. The opening, three short notes and a long one hammered out by the whole orchestra, is the most famous beginning in music, and the symphony's journey from that C minor storm to a blazing C major finale with trombones and piccolo became the model for a century of symphonies that end in triumph. The page shown is the first leaf of Beethoven's own manuscript, kept at the Berlin State Library. The visitor hears the first movement, Allegro con brio, played by the Fulda Symphonic Orchestra under Simon Schindler in a 2002 recording the orchestra released into the public domain.
facts: The 1808 premiere concert also introduced the Sixth Symphony, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy, with Beethoven himself at the piano.
Beethoven's secretary Anton Schindler claimed the composer said of the opening, 'Thus Fate knocks at the door', a story most scholars doubt.
The autograph score is one of the treasures of the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin, which has digitised it page by page.

artworks.title: Fourier series
artworks.medium: Epicycles, drawn live
artworks.description: Any repeating shape, Fourier claimed, is a sum of pure sine waves. He needed it to solve how heat spreads through a solid, and his 1822 Théorie analytique de la chaleur made the claim stick, though it took a century of analysis to say exactly when it is true. The panel shows it as circles riding on circles: the first turns once a cycle, the next three times as fast at a third the size, the next five times at a fifth, and so on. The tip of the last circle traces, as it goes, a square wave, the corners sharpening with every circle added. The same idea takes music apart into its overtones, images into frequencies, and is what every signal, from a phone call to a JPEG, passes through.
facts: Seven terms are drawn here; a perfect square wave would need infinitely many.
Ptolemy used circles on circles to predict planets; Fourier's are the same geometry, pointed at a different question.
Fourier was also the first, in 1824, to describe what is now called the greenhouse effect.
The fast Fourier transform of 1965 made the sum cheap enough to compute everywhere.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/fourier.ts: seven circles turning at odd multiples of one speed, their radii shrinking as 1/n, the tip drawing a square wave. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

location.name: Paris

artworks.medium: Nocturne for solo piano; engraved first edition
artworks.description: Chopin wrote the three Nocturnes of Opus 9 between 1830 and 1832, in the years he left Warsaw for Vienna and then settled in Paris, and they were his first nocturnes to be published, in Leipzig and Paris in 1832-33. He dedicated them to Marie Pleyel, the pianist wife of his publisher and piano maker Camille Pleyel. The second, in E-flat major, is the most played piece he ever wrote: a slow waltz-like accompaniment under a singing melody that returns three times, each time more elaborately ornamented, in the manner of an Italian opera aria. It fixed the idea of the nocturne, a short night piece for piano, that John Field had invented. The sheet shown is the title page of the Paris first edition issued by Maurice Schlesinger. The visitor hears the nocturne played by Frank Lévy in a Musopen recording released into the public domain.
facts: The nocturnes were printed by Kistner in Leipzig and Schlesinger in Paris in 1832-33, and by Wessel in London.
Chopin's pupils recorded many of his own improvised variants of the ornaments, so no two early editions agree on every note.
The dedicatee, Marie Pleyel (née Moke), was a celebrated virtuoso who had earlier been engaged to Berlioz.

artworks.title: Darwin's 'I think' tree of life sketch, Notebook B
artworks.medium: Pen and ink in a leather-bound pocket notebook
artworks.description: 'I think', and then a spindly branching diagram: a page from the pocket notebook Darwin opened in July 1837, nine months after the Beagle brought him home. He was twenty-eight and writing only for himself. The '1' at the base is a common ancestor; the branches ending in cross-bars are living species, the bare ones have died out. Underneath he reasons it through: if one ancestor is to give rise to as many living forms as exist now, and to groups of similar species, then extinction must be part of the process, and the gaps between living genera, 'A and B', 'C and B', record how long ago their lines parted. It is the first drawing of the tree of life as a genealogy rather than a ladder of perfection, and it came twenty-two years before On the Origin of Species, whose single illustration is a tidied version of this sketch. Darwin kept the notebooks all his life; this one is now in Cambridge University Library.
facts: Notebook B is the first of a series Darwin lettered B to E on the 'transmutation of species', kept from 1837 to 1839.
Darwin did not read Malthus, whose essay on population gave him the mechanism of natural selection, until September 1838, after this sketch.
The notebook measures about the size of a hand and travelled in Darwin's pocket; some pages were later cut out and reused.
The one figure in On the Origin of Species (1859) is a branching diagram descended from this page.

artworks.title: 'Au clair de la lune' phonautogram

date.label: 9 April 1860 (date written on the phonautogram sheet)

location.name: Paris
location.institution: Académie des sciences (the 1860 phonautogram sheets, deposited by Scott in 1861)

artworks.medium: Phonautogram: sound-wave trace scratched by a stylus into lampblack on paper; recovered as audio in 2008
artworks.description: Seventeen years before Edison's phonograph, a Parisian typesetter and amateur scientist, Édouard-Léon Scott de Martinville, built a machine that wrote sound down. His phonautograph gathered sound in a horn, let it shake a membrane, and had a hog's bristle scratch the vibration into lampblack on paper turning on a cylinder. Scott wanted a way to read speech from the squiggle; he never imagined playing it back. On 9 April 1860 he sang a few seconds of the folk song 'Au clair de la lune' into the horn and dated the sheet. In 2008 the First Sounds group had the trace scanned at high resolution and turned back into sound by computer at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, and the thin, wavering voice that emerged is the oldest recording of a human voice that can be recognised. The drawing shown is Scott's own sketch of his machine from his 1859 patent papers. The visitor hears the eleven-second 2008 recovery.
facts: The sheet was deposited with the Académie des sciences in Paris in 1861 and lay unplayed for 147 years.
The first 2008 playback ran at the wrong speed and was taken for a girl's voice; correcting the cylinder speed revealed a slow male voice, probably Scott's own.
Scott patented the phonautograph on 25 March 1857; Edison's phonograph, the first machine that could play sound back, followed in 1877.

artworks.title: Maxwell's equations

date.label: 1865 (A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field)

artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Electricity, magnetism and light in four lines: charges make electric fields, there are no magnetic charges, a changing magnetic field makes an electric one, and currents or changing electric fields make magnetic ones. Maxwell read the theory to the Royal Society in December 1864 and published it in 1865; from the equations fell a wave travelling at the speed of light, so light had to be an electromagnetic wave. Radio, the transistor further along, and every screen this museum is seen on, follow from here.
facts: Maxwell's own paper had twenty equations in twenty variables; the four vector equations shown are Oliver Heaviside's recasting of 1884 and 1885.
Heinrich Hertz produced and detected the predicted waves in 1887, eight years after Maxwell's death, and said they were of no use whatsoever.
Einstein kept a portrait of Maxwell on his study wall, beside Faraday and Newton, and called the theory 'the most profound and fruitful that physics has experienced since Newton'.

contributed.note: Typeset by 20watts from the TeX in the record with MathJax, with a figure drawn for this museum; the rendering is CC0, the equation itself is not subject to copyright.

artworks.title: The Galton board
artworks.medium: Balls and pegs, simulated live
artworks.description: Balls drop through rows of pegs, bouncing left or right at each with even odds, and pile up below. Each ball's fate is pure chance; the pile is not. It settles every time into the same bell-shaped curve, the normal distribution, because the sum of many small independent chances always does: that is the central limit theorem, and Francis Galton built this board in 1873 to make it something you could see. He called it the quincunx, after the pattern of the pegs. It is the shape of measurement error, of heights in a population, of noise in a signal, and the reason so much of statistics assumes a bell. The dashed line over the pile is the curve the arithmetic predicts; the balls are finding it on their own.
facts: Twelve rows of pegs give thirteen bins; the odds of the far bins are one in 4,096.
Galton showed the board at the Royal Institution in 1874.
He also used it to argue, wrongly as it turned out, that human traits must revert to the mean of a fixed population.
The same curve appears when the pegs are replaced by anything random enough: dice, rounding errors, the heights of soldiers.

contributed.note: Run live by src/sims/galton.ts: each ball takes twelve coin-flip turns through the pegs and lands in a bin; the binomial curve is drawn over the pile and the board empties when a bin fills. The program is the museum's own, CC0.

artworks.title: Boltzmann's entropy formula
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Entropy is the logarithm of the number of ways, W, that the atoms of a system can be arranged without changing what it looks like from outside. With this, Boltzmann, then a professor in Graz, explained in 1877 why heat flows one way and why the second law of thermodynamics is a law of probability: there are simply far more disordered arrangements than ordered ones. It is the bridge between the world of atoms, which most physicists of his day did not believe in, and the world of steam engines.
facts: The formula in this form, with the constant k, was first written down by Max Planck in 1900; Planck named k Boltzmann's constant.
It is carved on Boltzmann's gravestone in Vienna's Zentralfriedhof.
Boltzmann fought the sceptics of atoms for decades; Einstein's 1905 paper on Brownian motion, and Perrin's experiments, settled the matter soon after his death.

artworks.title: The Horse in Motion: Sallie Gardner at a Gallop
artworks.titleOriginal: The Horse in Motion. "Sallie Gardner," owned by Leland Stanford; running at a 1:40 gait over the Palo Alto track, 19th June 1878

madeIn.name: Palo Alto Stock Farm (Leland Stanford's farm, now the Stanford campus)

location.name: Washington, D.C.
location.institution: Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division (cabinet card; this animation was made from its scan)

artworks.medium: Twelve wet-plate photographs taken by electrically tripped cameras, published as a cabinet card; shown here as a reconstructed silent animation
artworks.description: On 19 June 1878, at Leland Stanford's stock farm at Palo Alto, Eadweard Muybridge lined up twelve cameras along a track, each with a shutter tripped by a thread the horse broke as it passed. The mare Sallie Gardner, running at about forty kilometres an hour, took the twelve pictures herself in under half a second. Stanford wanted to settle an old argument: does a galloping horse ever have all four feet off the ground? The plates showed that it does, but with the legs gathered under the body, not stretched out fore and aft as painters had always drawn them. Muybridge sold the sequence as a cabinet card and, from 1880, spun the frames on a glass disc in his zoopraxiscope so that audiences could watch the horse run. That projector is a direct ancestor of cinema, and the stop-motion study of movement he began here filled the eleven volumes of Animal Locomotion in 1887. What is shown here is a modern animation of the eleven usable frames of the 1878 card.
facts: The exposures were about a thousandth of a second, far faster than any studio portrait of the day.
Stanford paid for the work; the legend that it settled a $25,000 bet is unproven.
Muybridge's zoopraxiscope projections of 1880 were among the first moving pictures shown to a paying public.
Muybridge had been acquitted of murdering his wife's lover in 1875, three years before this sequence.

artworks.title: Lilienthal Normalsegelapparat (Deutsches Museum replica)
artworks.medium: Hang glider: willow and bamboo frame covered with waxed cotton, folding wings
artworks.description: The first aircraft ever produced in series and sold: Otto Lilienthal's 'normal soaring apparatus' of 1894, a hang glider of willow, bamboo and waxed cotton weighing 20 kg, which he flew from an artificial hill he built in Berlin-Lichterfelde and from the Gollenberg near Stölln. Lilienthal made some two thousand glides in his machines, the first repeated, controlled flights by a human being, and sold at least nine of this model for 500 marks each. He died on 10 August 1896, the day after a crash in one. This is a scan of the Deutsches Museum's replica, built by the museum in 1958 after the original from Lilienthal's estate had decayed.
facts: The Wright brothers began with Lilienthal's tables of lift; the 1903 Flyer in the next row is where his line of work led.
Buyers of the production glider included Nikolai Zhukovsky in Moscow and the publisher William Randolph Hearst; originals survive in London, Washington and Moscow.
The pilot hung by the forearms in the frame and steered by swinging the body; the wings fold for transport, and a bow at the front cushioned crashes.

artworks.title: Arrival of a Train at La Ciotat Station
artworks.titleOriginal: L'Arrivée d'un train en gare de La Ciotat

date.label: first shown 25 January 1896, Lyon; this print is the summer 1897 remake (Lumière catalogue no. 653)

artworks.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 50 seconds, shot with the Cinématographe Lumière
artworks.description: Fifty seconds, one fixed camera, no cut: a steam train pulls into the station at La Ciotat, on the coast east of Marseille where the Lumière family had a summer house, and passengers step down onto the platform. Louis Lumière set the Cinématographe at the platform's edge so that the locomotive grows from a speck to fill the frame and passes within arm's reach, a diagonal that still makes audiences lean back. The story that the first viewers fled screaming is a legend; the film was not even on the programme of the Lumières' first public show in Paris on 28 December 1895, and was first screened in Lyon in January 1896. It was popular enough that the brothers reshot it twice on the same platform; the version seen here, catalogue number 653, was taken in the summer of 1897 with Lumière children among the waiting passengers. The Cinématographe weighed five kilograms, was cranked by hand, and served as camera, printer and projector.
facts: Shown at about 16 frames a second from a reel of 17 metres: the length of one Lumière film.
Auguste and Louis Lumière ran their father's photographic-plate factory in Lyon; the camera was patented in February 1895.
By 1897 the Lumière catalogue listed over a thousand 'views' shot by operators across the world.
The film entered the public domain in France only on 1 January 2025, seventy years after Auguste Lumière's death.

artworks.title: Maple Leaf Rag
artworks.medium: Rag for solo piano; printed sheet music
artworks.description: Scott Joplin, the son of a formerly enslaved railway labourer, was playing piano in the Maple Leaf Club in Sedalia, Missouri, when the local music dealer John Stark published his 'Maple Leaf Rag' in September 1899. Joplin's contract gave him a royalty of one cent a copy, unusual for a Black composer at the time, and the piece went on to sell hundreds of thousands of copies, the first instrumental sheet music to do so. Its four sixteen-bar strains, with a syncopated right hand bouncing over a steady marching left hand, became the pattern for classic ragtime and the first distinctly American popular music to spread around the world. The cover shown is the 1899 Sedalia first edition. The visitor hears the United States Marine Band's 1906 recording, among the earliest ever made of the piece, which as a pre-1926 federal recording is in the public domain.
facts: Joplin's royalty contract with Stark, signed on 10 August 1899, is one of the earliest surviving royalty agreements for a Black American composer.
Joplin himself recorded the rag on piano rolls in 1916, a year before his death, when illness had already affected his playing.
The rag was published in Sedalia; Stark moved his firm to St. Louis the next year as sales took off.

artworks.title: A Trip to the Moon

location.name: Paris
location.institution: Cinémathèque française and others; the only known hand-coloured print was restored by Lobster Films in 2011

artworks.medium: 35 mm silent film, about 14 minutes at 14 frames a second, 260 metres, with painted sets and in-camera effects
artworks.description: Six astronomers are fired from a giant cannon in a bullet-shaped shell, land in the eye of the Man in the Moon, fight the Selenites with umbrellas, and fall back to Earth to a hero's welcome. Georges Méliès, a Paris stage magician who had bought a projector in 1896, made it in his glass-walled studio at Montreuil over the summer of 1902, playing the lead astronomer himself and painting the cardboard Moon. At fourteen minutes and thirty tableaux it was the longest and most expensive film he had attempted, and it was his biggest success, sold worldwide and pirated almost at once in the United States by Thomas Edison's agents. The shot of the shell stuck in the Moon's eye has become the emblem of early cinema. Méliès's business collapsed in the 1910s; he burned many of his negatives and ended up selling toys at the Gare Montparnasse before he was rediscovered and honoured in 1929. A hand-coloured print, found in Barcelona in 1993, was restored in 2011.
facts: Loosely based on Jules Verne's From the Earth to the Moon (1865) and H. G. Wells's The First Men in the Moon (1901).
Méliès used stop-substitution, dissolves and painted perspective; the Moon's approach was done by moving the camera on a trolley toward a painted face.
Edison's company copied the film and sold it in America without paying Méliès a cent, a loss he complained of all his life.
The film was added to the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2002, its centenary year.

The 12-horsepower engine was built from scratch in six weeks by the Wrights' mechanic Charlie Taylor, with a cast-aluminium crankcase.
The Flyer joined the Smithsonian collection in 1948 after a long dispute between Orville Wright and the Institution over who flew first.

artworks.title: Clair de lune
artworks.medium: Piece for solo piano, third movement of the Suite bergamasque; engraved first edition
artworks.description: Debussy sketched the four pieces of his Suite bergamasque around 1890, when he was twenty-eight and almost unknown, but he put them aside. Fifteen years later, now famous for Pelléas et Mélisande and La mer, he was persuaded by the publisher Fromont to revise and release them, and the suite appeared in Paris in 1905. The third piece, originally called 'Promenade sentimentale', was renamed 'Clair de lune' after a poem by Paul Verlaine in which masked revellers sing 'in the calm moonlight, sad and beautiful'. Its hushed opening in D-flat major, with chords that float rather than progress, became the best-known example of the new harmonic language later called impressionist, and one of the most loved piano pieces ever written. The page shown is the first page of the 1905 Fromont edition. The visitor hears the piece played by the Dutch pianist Laurens Goedhart, who released his 2011 recording under a Creative Commons Attribution licence.
facts: The title comes from Verlaine's poem 'Clair de lune' in Fêtes galantes (1869), which Debussy also set twice as a song.
The word 'bergamasque' refers to a rustic dance from Bergamo mentioned in the same poem.
Debussy never recorded the piece; his few piano rolls, made in 1913, are of other works.

artworks.title: Mass–energy equivalence
artworks.medium: Equation, typeset
artworks.description: Mass and energy are the same thing in different units, and the exchange rate is the speed of light squared. Einstein, a 26-year-old examiner at the Swiss patent office in Bern, derived it in a three-page afterthought to his special relativity paper, received by Annalen der Physik on 27 September 1905. The rate is so large that the mass lost by the Sun each second lights the Earth, and a gram of matter, fully converted, would power a city for a day.
facts: Einstein's paper is titled 'Does the inertia of a body depend on its energy content?' and writes the relation as L/V², with L for energy and V for the speed of light; the form E = mc² came later.
1905 was Einstein's annus mirabilis: four papers, on the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion, special relativity and this.
The first direct test came in 1932, when Cockcroft and Walton split lithium nuclei and found the energy released matched the mass lost.

artworks.title: Einstein, 'On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies', first page

location.institution: Printed journal (Annalen der Physik vol. 17, pp. 891-921); this scan is the Internet Archive's serials microfilm copy sim_annalen-der-physik_1905_17_5

artworks.medium: Letterpress printing on paper, journal page
artworks.description: The first page of the paper in which a twenty-six-year-old patent clerk in Bern replaced Newton's absolute space and time. Einstein starts from an everyday puzzle: moving a magnet past a coil or the coil past the magnet gives the same current, yet the physics of the day described the two cases differently. From that he takes two assumptions, that the laws of physics are the same for every observer moving at constant speed and that light travels at the same speed for all of them, and works out the consequences in thirty pages: moving clocks run slow, moving rods shrink, events simultaneous for one observer are not for another, and nothing with mass reaches the speed of light. The paper cites no earlier work and thanks only his friend Michele Besso. It reached the Annalen der Physik on 30 June 1905 and appeared on 26 September; a three-page sequel in November added the equation later written as E = mc². The theory became known as special relativity when Einstein generalised it to gravity in 1915.
facts: One of four papers Einstein published in 1905, his 'miracle year', alongside the photoelectric effect, Brownian motion and E = mc².
Written outside any university: Einstein was a 'technical expert, third class' at the Swiss patent office.
The word 'relativity' appears only as the 'principle of relativity'; Einstein did not name the theory.
The equations rediscovered Lorentz's transformations but gave them a wholly new meaning: there is no ether and no absolute rest.
